seeds: Computing includes designing software, constructing hardware, and organizing information systems for practical problems.
Covers several computing disciplines and their different kinds of work.
Do not present ACM's older five-part list as an exhaustive current taxonomy.
The same multi-byte number is stored in different byte orders under big-endian and little-endian conventions.
The example shows reversed significance ordering across memory addresses.
Byte order differs from the order of bits within one byte.
Virtual addresses translate to physical memory, allowing separate processes to use identical addresses without sharing the same physical pages.
Benefits and private address spaces; lines 31–50
Explains translation and isolated process mappings.
Windows is the inspected example; avoid claiming identical memory limits across systems.
Caches exploit repeated or nearby memory accesses by keeping recently accessed data in faster storage.
Connects locality to fast SRAM and slower main memory.
Cache benefits depend on access patterns; misses still require slower storage.
Public-key cryptography separates public and private keys, enabling encryption or verifiable signatures with different key roles.
Defines paired keys and separate encryption/signature operations.
Do not imply every public-key algorithm supports both encryption and signing.
Diffie–Hellman combines each party's private key with the other's public key to calculate a shared secret.
The equations show both parties compute the same secret from different private/public inputs.
Key agreement alone is not a claim that peers are authenticated; historical RFC is not modern deployment advice.
A recursive function solves smaller instances by calling itself and stops when a base case is reached.
Self-calls continue until the stopping condition.
A base case must be reachable; recursion does not always terminate.
SVG describes vector images in editable XML text, allowing clean scaling and scripted behavior.
Describes vector scaling and text-based XML representation.
The scaling claim concerns vector content; embedded raster images retain their raster limits.
Raspberry Pi exposes configurable GPIO pins so software can read digital inputs and control outputs.
Input/output modes connect the computer to external components.
Family entry; pin counts and electrical capabilities vary by model. Avoid direct motor-drive instructions.
Deep Blue combined parallel chess search, position evaluation, and grandmaster game data rather than relying on one technique.
Authors list search hardware, parallelism, evaluation and game databases.
This explains the historical system; avoid claims of human-like thought.
Microeconomics studies households, workers, and firms, including how they choose spending, work, prices, and production.
§1.2 opening comparison and Microeconomics subsection; lines 32–43
Distinguishes individual decision-makers from economy-wide measures.
A broad field entry, distinct from the separate Macroeconomics identity.
Comparative advantage depends on what production gives up, rather than who produces more with the same resources.
Defines lower cost in terms of other goods.
Avoid unconditional promises that every person benefits from actual trade policies.
Public goods are hard to exclude people from using, and one person's use does not diminish another's use.
Both nonexcludability and non-rivalry are required.
Government funding alone does not make a good a public good.
Economies of scale reduce average cost as production expands while all inputs can vary in the long run.
Economies of Scale and long-run distinction; lines 65–99
Distinguishes long-run scale from changing one short-run input.
Larger production need not always lower cost; diseconomies can follow.
Economic elasticity compares percentage changes; price elasticity measures how quantity responds to price changes.
Percentage definitions and slope comparison; lines 29–30 and 82–89
Demand and supply examples use percentage ratios.
The selected identity is general economic elasticity; price response is an example, not its only form.
Marginal cost measures the additional cost of extra output, unlike average cost spread across all units.
Defines marginal cost using changes in cost and quantity.
Discrete batches use cost change divided by output change.
Fixed costs, such as a signed factory lease, stay unchanged as output changes over the relevant short run.
Lease example preserves the time horizon.
Costs can change after the lease or planning period; not permanently fixed.
Simultaneous deposit withdrawals can overwhelm a bank's ability to turn long-term assets into cash, even when assets exceed liabilities.
Explains why solvency does not guarantee immediate liquidity.
Mechanism only; no prediction about a particular bank or current depositor action.
The World Bank Group divides development work among five institutions, including government lending and private-sector investment.
Five Organizations One World Bank Group; lines 68–130
Lists five distinct organizations and functions.
World Bank Group is broader than the World Bank (IBRD and IDA); do not conflate those IDs.
Civil engineering designs and maintains shared infrastructure, including bridges, drinking-water networks, and transport systems.
Names infrastructure examples spanning structures, transport and water.
The field includes both construction and ongoing maintenance.
A turbofan splits incoming air between an engine core and a bypass stream; both streams contribute thrust.
Distinguishes bypass fan flow from air entering combustion.
Avoid a universal efficiency or bypass-ratio claim.
Fly-by-wire sends pilot commands electrically to actuators; digital versions use computers instead of direct mechanical control linkages.
Digital signals replacing rods and cables; lines 255–263
Shows a digital example replacing mechanical cockpit connections.
The general identity also includes analog systems; do not define all fly-by-wire as digital.
A suspension bridge transfers deck loads through hangers to main cables, towers, and anchored foundations.
Anatomy of a Suspension Bridge; lines 32–47
The described load path links deck to ground.
The Golden Gate Bridge is the inspected example; avoid claiming all designs use identical anchorages.
Cantilever bridge arms project from supporting towers or piers; at the Forth Bridge they connect through suspended spans.
The heritage statement describes projecting arms and connecting suspended spans.
Specific dimensions and steel details belong to the Forth example, not every cantilever bridge.
Bearings support relative motion and transmit forces; rolling bearings separate moving rings with balls or rollers rather than a sliding surface.
Separates the support/load function from different friction mechanisms.
Not all bearings use rolling elements; plain and other types remain part of the identity.
On a derailleur bicycle, a smaller front chainring or larger rear cog makes pedaling easier by changing gearing.
Shows the opposing effects of front and rear sprocket sizes.
This example concerns a conventional chain-and-derailleur drivetrain; hub gearing differs.
Epicyclic or planetary gearing shares transmitted loads among several planet gears, supporting high torque capacity.
Planetary systems and load sharing; PDF p.3, lines 456–471
Manufacturer explains why several planet gears can carry a larger load.
Do not treat the illustrated product ratios as universal epicyclic ratios.
Bus rapid transit combines protected bus lanes with rapid-transit features such as off-board fares and platform-level boarding.
Identifies corridor design and boarding/payment elements.
Features vary by system; the ITDP Standard is an explicit evaluation framework.
Singapore's MRT includes the North East Line, an early fully automated underground heavy-rail line designed as part of integrated public transport.
Ahead of its time and train features; lines 7–38
Explains automation and integration within the MRT system.
Automation claim is about the North East Line example; do not imply every MRT line is driverless.
Portal makes linked openings into a puzzle tool for moving both the player and objects through space.
Valve explicitly describes physical puzzles solved by opening portals for objects and the player.
The source describes Portal, not its sequel or arbitrary real-world teleportation.
Minecraft changes building constraints by mode: Survival requires gathered materials, while Creative supplies blocks immediately.
Building in Creative vs. Survival mode, lines 557–567
The developer contrasts mined building resources with immediate block availability.
The comparison is between standard Survival and Creative, not every custom game mode.
Tetris turns falling-piece placement into line clearing: a completely filled horizontal row disappears.
Official instructions require rotation and placement of Tetriminos to complete rows without gaps.
Do not generalize variant scoring or speed rules beyond this core mechanic.
Outside castling, a chess king moves to an adjacent square that an opponent does not attack.
The official rule gives adjacent movement and excludes attacked destinations; the next section establishes castling as an exception.
Keep the castling exception; ordinary movement is not the king's only legal move.
A chess queen travels along ranks, files, or diagonals, but cannot jump over intervening pieces.
The queen movement rule incorporates the rule against crossing occupied squares.
Destinations still obey general legality and occupancy rules; this is a movement pattern, not a complete move validator.
High jump uses a one-foot takeoff to clear an elevated horizontal bar without dislodging it.
What is the high jump?, lines 196–198
World Athletics describes the takeoff, clearance objective, and landing mat.
Do not imply that a particular clearance technique is compulsory.
In stadium relays, baton exchange is judged by the baton's position within the takeover zone, not simply the runners' bodies.
The rule defines the exchange from first receiving contact to sole possession and locates the entire baton.
Qualify the stadium baton example; relay race is broader than this athletics rule and zone lengths differ.
Triple jump follows hop, step, and jump: the hop lands on the takeoff foot, then the step lands on the other.
The rules state the sequence and distinguish same-foot from other-foot landings.
This explains the prescribed sequence, not a training technique or performance guarantee.
Curling stones curve as they slide; players apply rotation at release to control the direction of that curve.
Turns, Release and Line of Delivery, printed p.34, lines 984–987
The national federation's guide connects stone rotation at release with direction of curl.
Avoid claiming a settled microscopic explanation of curling or that every form allows sweeping.
Phonetics studies speech as physical sound: how bodies produce it and which acoustic properties listeners receive.
The lesson distinguishes articulatory study of bodily production from acoustic study of sound waves.
Use speech as the concrete focus here; do not claim that modern phonetics excludes signed-language modality.
A morpheme is a smallest meaningful unit; dogs contains dog and a plural ending despite having only one syllable.
SIL explicitly contrasts two meaningful units with one syllable in dogs.
Morphemes need not correspond to syllables or stand alone as words.
Assimilation makes a speech sound more like a nearby sound, with influence possible from either a preceding or following segment.
The lesson defines similarity to neighboring sounds and distinguishes anticipatory from perseveratory influence.
This is phonological assimilation, not cultural assimilation.
Grammatical aspect presents an event as ongoing or complete, whereas tense locates it relative to time.
The lesson separates temporal location from the perspective taken on an event, including English progressive forms.
Aspect distinctions and their grammatical marking vary across languages; English perfect and perfective are not interchangeable labels.
Code-switching alternates languages within a conversation or utterance, so language-processing systems must handle more than one language together.
The authors define alternation within conversation or utterance and motivate processing code-switched speech and text.
Use the multilingual sense inspected here; broader social uses of the phrase are outside this source.
A register groups language by situation of use, such as conversation or research methods, rather than simply by speaker community.
The authors define situational varieties and distinguish them from dialects associated with speaker groups.
This is the authors' functional register framework; not every sociolinguistic theory draws the same boundary.
English Braille can spell letters individually or use contractions that represent frequent words and letter groups.
What Is Braille? and Contracted and Uncontracted Braille, lines 9–16 and 49–59
BANA describes six-dot cells, character meanings, and contracted versus uncontracted English text.
English Braille is the broad identity; UEB is the inspected contemporary example, not a synonym for all historical English codes.
American Sign Language uses hands and facial movement with its own grammar, rather than reproducing English word for word.
What is American Sign Language?, lines 22–24
The NIH institute identifies ASL as a natural language expressed with hands and face and with grammar different from English.
ASL is not a universal sign language; other regions have different signed languages.
Montessori practice arranges accessible materials so children choose an activity, work with it, and restore it before choosing again.
The society describes accessible learning materials and the child's choose-use-clean-up cycle.
The inspected example concerns infant and toddler classrooms; it does not establish comparative educational outcomes.
Classical conditioning lets a previously neutral cue elicit a learned response after it is paired with another stimulus.
The text traces tone-food pairing and later salivation to the tone alone.
The example concerns stimulus association; do not equate it with reinforcement of voluntary actions.
Operant conditioning changes future behavior through its consequences: reinforcement increases a behavior's likelihood, while punishment decreases it.
The text defines behavior-consequence association and the direction of reinforcement and punishment.
Negative reinforcement removes a stimulus to increase behavior; it is not another name for punishment.
Gestalt psychology studies organized perception; nearby dots, for example, tend to appear as groups rather than isolated inputs.
OpenStax connects Gestalt's organized-whole account to the proximity grouping principle.
Proximity is one example, not an exhaustive account of the historical school.
Executive functions help people plan, focus attention, switch between demands, and coordinate tasks.
Harvard describes planning, attention, shifting, juggling tasks, and information management.
This is a group of cognitive skills, not a single brain switch or a measure of personal virtue.
Conformity can mean following a group's behavior without privately agreeing; people may seek acceptance or trust the group's information.
The text distinguishes going along, normative acceptance, and informational reliance.
These are mechanisms and possibilities; do not imply that everyone conforms in every group.
A mnemonic organizes recall cues; the acronym HOMES uses initials to cue the five Great Lakes.
The text defines memory aids and explicitly gives HOMES as an acronym example.
A mnemonic provides cues; it does not guarantee accurate recall or understanding.
Forgetting can reflect interference: older information blocks new recall, or newer information competes with an older memory.
The passage distinguishes proactive and retroactive interference and notes inaccessible stored information.
Interference is one cause of forgetting; failure to recall does not by itself prove permanent erasure.
Self-concept is how someone thinks and feels about themselves; Rogers distinguished the perceived real self from an ideal self.
The text defines self-concept and gives Rogers's real-versus-ideal distinction.
Attribute the distinction to Rogers; avoid presenting his claims about health or parenting as established universal effects.
Social psychology examines how other people and social situations shape thoughts, feelings, and actions alongside individual characteristics.
The section covers interpersonal influence, situational interpretation, and modern attention to both person and situation.
Do not imply that situations determine all behavior or that personality is irrelevant.
Social stratification ranks groups through unequal resources and status, rather than merely describing individual differences.
The passage connects social rankings with wealth, income, education, background and power.
Ranking systems and relevant resources vary across societies.
Social mobility can move people up or down; intergenerational comparisons track parents and children, while intragenerational comparisons track one lifetime.
Defines mobility and distinguishes upward, downward, intergenerational and intragenerational changes.
Mobility is possible without being equally accessible or common in every system.
Cultural relativism interprets a culture using its own standards; understanding a practice does not require endorsing it.
Cultural relativism and critical evaluation; lines 80–85
Contrasts cultural relativism with judging another culture through one's own standards.
Do not imply that interpretation prevents criticism or requires accepting every practice.
Fictive kinship recognizes family ties through social commitment without requiring biological ancestry; godparenthood provides one example.
The section describes intentional family relationships and godparenthood.
Fictive does not mean fake; a godparent may also be a biological relative.
Symbolic interactionism examines how people create and interpret shared meanings through everyday interactions.
The theory emphasizes communication, symbols and meanings formed and interpreted through interaction.
Present this as a theoretical perspective, not a claim that one mechanism explains all society.
Socialization is lifelong learning of a group's norms, beliefs and values; changing workplaces can require learning new expectations.
Socialization definition and workplace example; lines 48–55
The workplace example and definition show social learning beyond childhood.
Socialization is broader than casual socializing and does not end in childhood.
Universal design accommodates diverse users through choices such as perceptible information, flexible use and reduced physical effort.
The principles describe equivalent access, user options, understandable information and comfortable use.
The principles guide design; no single design necessarily meets every user's needs.
Internet Archive's Wayback Machine lets people inspect captured webpages by URL and date, though an archived site can contain gaps.
URL/date search and incomplete captures; lines 12–16, 57–69
The help page explains URL/date searches and warns that missing captures may lead to another date or the live web.
One service illustrates the institution; avoid claiming comprehensive or complete archival coverage.
UNICEF supports childhood immunization by procuring cold-chain equipment that protects vaccines during storage and transport.
Temperature protection and UNICEF procurement; lines 64–80
The passage describes equipment and services UNICEF procures with governments and partners.
This is one documented activity, not UNICEF's full mandate; storage requirements vary by vaccine.
